name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q01 - Contributions of Panchanan Maheshwari

questiontext.text: Which of the following scientific achievements is associated with the distinguished Indian botanist Panchanan Maheshwari?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Panchanan Maheshwari (1904–1966) was a renowned botanist who worked extensively on plant embryology, morphology, and tissue culture at the University of Delhi.

Step 2: Evaluation
He popularised the use of embryological characters in taxonomy, emphasised artificial culture of immature embryos, and gained worldwide acclaim for his work on test tube fertilisation and intra-ovarian pollination. He also led the publication of the first NCERT Biology textbooks for Higher Secondary Schools in 1964.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Test tube fertilisation and intra-ovarian pollination are key achievements credited to Panchanan Maheshwari.

answer.text: Test tube fertilisation and intra-ovarian pollination
Discovery of double fertilisation in angiosperms
Formulation of the five-kingdom classification system
Elucidation of the semi-conservative mode of DNA replication

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q02 - Life span and body size correlation

questiontext.text: Which pair of organisms best illustrates that the life spans of organisms are not necessarily correlated with their body sizes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
The period from birth to the natural death of an organism is called its life span. Life spans vary from a few days to a few thousand years and do not depend directly on the size of the organism.

Step 2: Evaluation
The body sizes of a crow and a parrot are not very different, yet their approximate life spans show a wide difference: a crow lives for about 15 years, whereas a parrot lives for about 140 years. Similarly, a mango tree has a much shorter life span than a peepal tree despite comparable sizes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Crow and parrot best demonstrate that life span is not necessarily correlated with body size.

answer.text: Butterfly and fruit fly
Crow and parrot
Elephant and tortoise
Rice plant and banyan tree

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q03 - Absence of natural death in single-celled organisms

questiontext.text: Single-celled organisms are considered biologically immortal because they do not undergo natural death. What is the primary reason for this?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Death of every individual organism is a certainty, except in single-celled organisms.

Step 2: Evaluation
In single-celled organisms such as Protists and Monerans, cell division itself is a mode of reproduction. The parent cell divides by mitosis (such as binary fission) into two daughter cells, continuing its existence in the progeny without leaving behind a dead parental body.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Single-celled organisms have no natural death because the parent body divides into daughter individuals through cell division.

answer.text: They lack cellular organelles that undergo senescence
They continuously form gametes by meiosis
The parent cell divides into two daughter individuals, so cell division is itself reproduction
They secrete a protective cyst that prevents ageing under all conditions

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q04 - Biological significance of reproduction

questiontext.text: Which biological process ensures the continuity of a species generation after generation despite the eventual death of every individual?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Individual organisms have finite life spans and eventually die, yet species persist over thousands of years.

Step 2: Evaluation
Reproduction is the biological process in which an organism gives rise to young ones (offspring) similar to itself. These offspring grow, mature, and produce new offspring, thereby maintaining a cycle of birth, growth, and death that ensures species continuity.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Reproduction is the process that enables the continuity of a species generation after generation.

answer.text: Senescence
Encystation
Metabolism
Reproduction

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q05 - Meaning of the term clone

questiontext.text: The term "clone" is used to describe offspring that are:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In asexual reproduction, a single parent produces offspring without the fusion of gametes from two different individuals.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because all offspring arise from a single parent through mitotic divisions, they are exact copies of the parent and of each other. Thus, they are both morphologically and genetically identical.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Clones are individuals that are morphologically and genetically similar to one another and to their parent.

answer.text: Morphologically and genetically similar to one another and to the parent
Morphologically similar but genetically distinct from the parent
Genetically identical to the parent but formed by syngamy
Morphologically different from each other due to meiosis

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q06 - Cell division as reproduction in Protists and Monerans

questiontext.text: In which of the following groups of organisms does the parent cell divide by mitosis into two to give rise to new individuals, making cell division itself a mode of reproduction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Asexual reproduction is common among single-celled organisms as well as plants and animals with relatively simple organisations.

Step 2: Evaluation
In Protists and Monerans, the organism or parent cell divides by mitosis into two halves to form new individuals directly. Hence, cell division is itself a mode of reproduction in these groups.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Cell division acts directly as a mode of reproduction in Protists and Monerans.

answer.text: Bryophytes and Pteridophytes
Protists and Monerans
Gymnosperms and Angiosperms
Reptiles and Birds

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q07 - Budding in yeast versus binary fission

questiontext.text: How does asexual cell division in yeast differ from binary fission in Amoeba and Paramecium?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Both binary fission and budding are modes of asexual reproduction in unicellular organisms.

Step 2: Evaluation
In Amoeba and Paramecium, binary fission divides a cell into two equal halves, each rapidly growing into an adult. In contrast, in yeast, cell division is unequal, producing small buds that initially remain attached to the parent cell and eventually separate to mature into new yeast cells.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Asexual reproduction in yeast involves unequal division producing small buds, unlike the equal division seen in binary fission.

answer.text: Yeast undergoes meiosis during budding, whereas Amoeba undergoes mitosis
Yeast forms motile zoospores, whereas Paramecium forms non-motile conidia
Division in yeast is unequal, producing small buds that initially remain attached to the parent cell
Yeast requires two parents for bud formation, whereas binary fission involves one parent

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q08 - Encystation and sporulation in Amoeba

questiontext.text: Which of the following accurately describes the events of encystation and sporulation in Amoeba?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Amoeba adapts to unfavourable environmental conditions through encystation and reproduces rapidly upon return of favourable conditions through sporulation.

Step 2: Evaluation
Under unfavourable conditions, Amoeba withdraws its pseudopodia and secretes a three-layered hard covering or cyst around itself (encystation). When favourable conditions return, the encysted Amoeba divides by multiple fission to produce many minute amoebae or pseudopodiospores; the cyst wall bursts out, liberating the spores into the surrounding medium (sporulation).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Encystation involves withdrawing pseudopodia and secreting a three-layered cyst under unfavourable conditions, while sporulation involves multiple fission to form pseudopodiospores when favourable conditions return.

answer.text: Encystation occurs during favourable conditions by secreting a single-layered cyst, followed by binary fission
Sporulation occurs during unfavourable conditions to form a three-layered cyst around pseudopodia
Encystation involves multiple fission to form zoospores, whereas sporulation involves unequal budding
Under unfavourable conditions, Amoeba withdraws pseudopodia and secretes a three-layered cyst; upon return of favourable conditions, it divides by multiple fission to liberate pseudopodiospores

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q09 - Zoospores as microscopic motile structures

questiontext.text: Which of the following asexual reproductive structures are typically microscopic and motile, commonly found in simple plants such as algae?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Members of Kingdom Fungi and simple plants such as algae reproduce through specialised asexual reproductive structures.

Step 2: Evaluation
The most common of these structures are zoospores, which are usually microscopic motile structures (such as in Chlamydomonas). In contrast, conidia (in Penicillium), buds (in Hydra), and gemmules (in sponges) are non-motile structures.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Zoospores are the microscopic motile asexual reproductive structures.

answer.text: Zoospores
Conidia
Gemmules
Bulbils

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q10 - Vegetative reproduction as asexual reproduction

questiontext.text: Why is vegetative propagation in plants—using structures such as runners, rhizomes, suckers, tubers, offsets, and bulbs—considered a type of asexual reproduction?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Reproduction is classified as asexual when offspring are produced by a single parent with or without gamete formation, without the participation of two parents.

Step 2: Evaluation
In plants, vegetative propagules such as runners, rhizomes, suckers, tubers, offsets, and bulbs give rise to new offspring from a single parent plant without involving two parents or gametic fusion. Hence, the resulting offspring are clones.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Vegetative propagation is a type of asexual reproduction because the formation of new offspring from vegetative propagules does not involve two parents.

answer.text: It involves meiosis in the vegetative propagules before sprouting
The formation of these structures and new offspring does not involve two parents
It always produces genetically variable offspring suited for adverse conditions
It requires pollination prior to the development of new plantlets

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q11 - Water hyacinth as Terror of Bengal

questiontext.text: The aquatic weed commonly known as the "terror of Bengal" causes the death of fishes in standing water bodies primarily because it:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Water hyacinth is an invasive aquatic weed introduced in India for its attractive flowers and leaf shape, which propagates vegetatively at a phenomenal rate via offsets.

Step 2: Evaluation
Because it spreads rapidly across standing water bodies, it drains dissolved oxygen from the water, which leads to the death of fishes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Water hyacinth causes fish mortality by draining oxygen from the water body.

answer.text: Releases toxic alkaloids into the water during flowering
Parasitises the gills of freshwater fishes
Propagates vegetatively at a phenomenal rate and drains oxygen from the water
Blocks gamete transfer in aquatic animals by releasing spores

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q12 - Site of origin of plantlets in vegetative propagules

questiontext.text: In cultivated plants such as potato, sugarcane, banana, and ginger, new plantlets invariably arise from which specific structure, and how does this differ from Bryophyllum?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Vegetative propagation in angiosperms occurs from specific meristematic regions capable of producing roots and shoots when in contact with damp soil or water.

Step 2: Evaluation
In potato (tuber eyes), sugarcane, banana, and ginger (rhizomes), new plantlets invariably arise from the nodes present in their modified stems. In contrast, in Bryophyllum, adventitious buds arise from the notches present at the margins of the leaves.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Plantlets arise from nodes of modified stems in potato, sugarcane, banana, and ginger, whereas they arise from adventitious buds in leaf margin notches in Bryophyllum.

answer.text: They arise from internodes of modified roots in potato and ginger, whereas in Bryophyllum they arise from the leaf petiole
They arise from floral buds in banana and sugarcane, whereas in Bryophyllum they arise from stem nodes
They arise from root tips in all four plants, whereas in Bryophyllum they arise from the leaf midrib
They arise from nodes present in the modified stems, whereas in Bryophyllum adventitious buds arise from notches at the leaf margins

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q13 - Fragmentation in Hydra

questiontext.text: When the body of an organism like Hydra breaks into distinct pieces and each piece grows into an adult capable of producing offspring, this mode of asexual reproduction is called:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Simple multicellular animals can reproduce asexually through body division or specialised outgrowths.

Step 2: Evaluation
When an organism's body breaks into distinct pieces (fragments) and each fragment grows into a complete adult capable of producing offspring, the process is termed fragmentation, as seen in Hydra.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
This mode of asexual reproduction is known as fragmentation.

answer.text: Fragmentation
Sporulation
Encystation
Parthenogenesis

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q14 - Shift to sexual reproduction in algae and fungi

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately describes the distribution of asexual and sexual modes of reproduction across organisms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Different groups of organisms rely on asexual and sexual reproduction depending on their complexity and environmental conditions.

Step 2: Evaluation
Organisms with relatively simple organisation, such as algae and fungi, commonly reproduce asexually, but they shift to the sexual mode of reproduction just before the onset of adverse conditions. Higher plants exhibit both asexual (vegetative) and sexual modes of reproduction, whereas most animals exhibit only the sexual mode of reproduction.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Algae and fungi shift from asexual to sexual reproduction just before adverse conditions begin, higher plants show both modes, and most animals show only sexual reproduction.

answer.text: Algae and fungi reproduce exclusively by sexual means throughout their life cycle
Algae and fungi shift to sexual reproduction just before adverse conditions, higher plants exhibit both modes, and most animals exhibit only sexual reproduction
Higher plants have lost the ability to reproduce asexually and rely solely on seeds
Most animals shift to asexual reproduction during adverse environmental conditions

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q15 - Juvenile and vegetative phase

questiontext.text: In plants, the period of growth and maturity that must be attained before sexual reproduction can begin is specifically termed the:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
All sexually reproducing organisms pass through a period of growth before they attain reproductive maturity.

Step 2: Evaluation
This period of growth is generally called the juvenile phase, and in plants it is specifically known as the vegetative phase. Its end marks the beginning of the reproductive phase, which is easily seen in higher plants when they come to flower.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In plants, this pre-reproductive growth period is called the vegetative phase.

answer.text: Senescent phase
Embryogenic phase
Vegetative phase
Resting phase

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q16 - Phases in annual, biennial, and perennial plants

questiontext.text: In which category of plants is it very difficult to clearly define the vegetative, reproductive, and senescent phases?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Flowering plants exhibit vegetative, reproductive, and senescent phases, but the clarity of boundaries between these phases varies with plant longevity.

Step 2: Evaluation
Annual and biennial plants show clear-cut vegetative, reproductive, and senescent phases. However, in perennial species, repeated cycles of growth and flowering make it very difficult to clearly demarcate these three phases.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
It is very difficult to clearly define these phases in perennial plant species.

answer.text: Annual plants only
Biennial plants only
Both annual and biennial plants
Perennial plant species

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q17 - Unusual flowering in bamboo and Strobilanthus kunthiana

questiontext.text: Which pair of plants correctly matches their unusual flowering periodicity as described in the text?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
A few plant species exhibit unusual flowering phenomena with very long vegetative periods.

Step 2: Evaluation
Bamboo species flower only once in their lifetime, generally after 50–100 years, produce a large number of fruits, and die. Strobilanthus kunthiana (neelakuranji) flowers once in 12 years; its mass flowering in September–October 2006 turned hilly areas of Kerala, Karnataka, and Tamil Nadu into blue stretches.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Bamboo species flower once in 50–100 years and die, whereas Strobilanthus kunthiana flowers once in 12 years.

answer.text: Bamboo species: once in 50–100 years; Strobilanthus kunthiana: once in 12 years
Bamboo species: once in 12 years; Strobilanthus kunthiana: once in 50–100 years
Bamboo species: annually; Strobilanthus kunthiana: once in 50–100 years
Bamboo species: once in 12 years; Strobilanthus kunthiana: biennially

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q18 - Egg laying in wild birds versus poultry farms

questiontext.text: Birds living in nature lay eggs only seasonally, whereas birds in captivity (such as poultry farms) can be made to lay eggs throughout the year. In the latter case, egg laying is:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In nature, egg laying in birds is a seasonal phenomenon tied to their reproductive phase.

Step 2: Evaluation
When birds in captivity are made to lay eggs throughout the year in poultry farms, this continuous egg laying is not related to natural reproduction; rather, it is a commercial exploitation for human welfare.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Year-round egg laying in captive poultry birds is not related to reproduction, but is commercial exploitation for human welfare.

answer.text: A shift from seasonal breeding to natural continuous sexual reproduction
Not related to reproduction, but is a commercial exploitation for human welfare
An example of parthenogenesis induced by captivity
A transition from oviparity to viviparity

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q19 - Oestrus cycle versus menstrual cycle in placental mammals

questiontext.text: Which of the following correctly compares the cyclical reproductive changes in females of placental mammals?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
During the reproductive phase, females of placental mammals exhibit cyclical changes in the activities of ovaries, accessory ducts, and hormones.

Step 2: Evaluation
In non-primate mammals such as cows, sheep, rats, deer, dogs, and tigers, these cyclical changes are called the oestrus cycle. In primates such as monkeys, apes, and humans, they are called the menstrual cycle. Mammals exhibiting these cycles only during favourable seasons are called seasonal breeders, while those reproductively active throughout their reproductive phase are called continuous breeders.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Non-primate placental mammals exhibit the oestrus cycle, whereas primates exhibit the menstrual cycle.

answer.text: Primates such as monkeys and humans exhibit the oestrus cycle, while cows and dogs exhibit the menstrual cycle
All seasonal breeders exhibit the menstrual cycle, whereas all continuous breeders exhibit the oestrus cycle
Non-primate mammals such as cows, sheep, rats, and tigers exhibit the oestrus cycle, while primates such as monkeys, apes, and humans exhibit the menstrual cycle
Cyclical changes occur only in the ovaries and not in accessory ducts or hormone levels

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q20 - Senescence and hormonal regulation of life phases

questiontext.text: In both plants and animals, what is responsible for the transitions between the juvenile, reproductive, and senescent phases?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Organisms pass sequentially through juvenile/vegetative, reproductive, and senescent phases, with the end of the reproductive phase serving as a parameter of senescence (old age), accompanied by concomitant changes like slowing of metabolism.

Step 2: Evaluation
In both plants and animals, hormones are responsible for the transitions between these three phases. Additionally, interaction between hormones and certain environmental factors regulates the reproductive processes and associated behavioural expressions.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Hormones are responsible for the transitions between the three phases in both plants and animals.

answer.text: Random genetic mutations alone
Meiotic division of somatic cells
Environmental temperature alone without internal regulation
Hormones (interacting with certain environmental factors)

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q21 - Isogametes and heterogametes

questiontext.text: In which organism are the two gametes so similar in appearance that it is not possible to categorise them into male and female gametes (homogametes/isogametes)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gametes may be morphologically indistinguishable (homogametes or isogametes) or morphologically distinct (heterogametes).

Step 2: Evaluation
In the alga Cladophora, the two gametes are identical in appearance and are called homogametes (isogametes). In contrast, Fucus (an alga) and Homo sapiens (human beings) produce morphologically distinct heterogametes (antherozoid/sperm and egg/ovum).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Homogametes (isogametes) are observed in Cladophora.

answer.text: Cladophora
Fucus
Homo sapiens
Marchantia

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q22 - Monoecious versus dioecious flowering plants

questiontext.text: Which of the following pairs consists exclusively of dioecious flowering plants?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In flowering plants, if both staminate (male) and pistillate (female) flowers are present on the same individual, the plant is monoecious. If they are borne on separate individuals, the plant is dioecious.

Step 2: Evaluation
Cucurbits and coconuts are examples of monoecious plants, whereas papaya and date palm are examples of dioecious plants.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Papaya and date palm are both dioecious flowering plants.

answer.text: Cucurbits and coconuts
Papaya and date palm
Cucurbits and papaya
Coconuts and date palm

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q23 - Hermaphrodite animals versus unisexual animals

questiontext.text: Which of the following groups of animals consists entirely of bisexual (hermaphrodite) organisms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Bisexual animals that possess both male and female reproductive organs in the same individual are called hermaphrodites, whereas species with separate male and female individuals are unisexual.

Step 2: Evaluation
Earthworm, sponge, tapeworm, and leech are typical examples of bisexual animals (hermaphrodites). In contrast, cockroach is a unisexual animal species.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Earthworm, sponge, tapeworm, and leech are all hermaphrodite animals.

answer.text: Earthworm, cockroach, and leech
Cockroach, sponge, and tapeworm
Earthworm, sponge, tapeworm, and leech
Tapeworm, cockroach, and frog

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q24 - Cell division during gamete formation in haploid and diploid parents

questiontext.text: Gametes are always haploid regardless of whether the parent body is haploid or diploid. Which statement correctly describes the type of cell division involved in gamete formation across different plant groups?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gametes are always haploid (\(n\)). Therefore, a haploid parent produces gametes by mitotic division, whereas a diploid parent must undergo meiosis (reduction division) via specialised meiocytes to produce haploid gametes.

Step 2: Evaluation
Several organisms belonging to monera, fungi, algae, and bryophytes have a haploid plant body and form gametes by mitosis. In contrast, organisms belonging to pteridophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms, and most animals have a diploid parental body and form haploid gametes by meiosis.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Haploid organisms such as algae and bryophytes produce gametes by mitosis, whereas diploid organisms such as pteridophytes, gymnosperms, and angiosperms produce gametes by meiosis in meiocytes.

answer.text: Algae and bryophytes have a diploid plant body and produce gametes by meiosis
Pteridophytes and gymnosperms have a haploid plant body and produce gametes by mitosis
All sexually reproducing organisms produce gametes exclusively by meiosis
Haploid parents (monera, fungi, algae, bryophytes) produce gametes by mitosis, whereas diploid parents (pteridophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms, most animals) produce gametes by meiosis in meiocytes

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q25 - Chromosome numbers in Ophioglossum, butterfly, potato, and apple

questiontext.text: If the chromosome number in a gamete (\(n\)) of Ophioglossum is 630, and the chromosome number in a meiocyte (\(2n\)) of a butterfly is 380, what are the chromosome numbers in a meiocyte of Ophioglossum and a gamete of a butterfly, respectively?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
For Ophioglossum (a fern), the haploid chromosome number in a gamete is \(n = 630\). For a butterfly, the diploid chromosome number in a meiocyte is \(2n = 380\).

Step 2: Relevant Formulae and Principles
In diploid organisms, meiocytes (\(2n\)) undergo meiosis to produce haploid gametes (\(n\)), so the chromosome number in a meiocyte is twice that in a gamete: \(2n = 2 \times n\), and \(n = \frac{2n}{2}\).

Step 3: Step-by-Step Working
For Ophioglossum: \(2n = 2 \times 630 = 1260\).
For butterfly: \(n = \frac{380}{2} = 190\).

Step 4: Final Answer
The chromosome number in a meiocyte of Ophioglossum is 1260, and in a gamete of a butterfly is 190.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q26 - Chromosome numbers in rat, onion, maize, and rice

questiontext.text: Given that the haploid chromosome number (\(n\)) in gametes of rice is 12 and in onion is 8, and the diploid chromosome number (\(2n\)) in meiocytes of maize is 20 and in apple is 34, which set correctly lists the missing values in the order: rice (\(2n\)), onion (\(2n\)), maize (\(n\)), apple (\(n\))?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Principles
Rice gamete \(n = 12\); onion gamete \(n = 8\); maize meiocyte \(2n = 20\); apple meiocyte \(2n = 34\). Because meiocytes are diploid (\(2n\)) and gametes are haploid (\(n\)), \(2n = 2 \times n\).

Step 2: Step-by-Step Working
Rice meiocyte: \(2n = 2 \times 12 = 24\).
Onion meiocyte: \(2n = 2 \times 8 = 16\).
Maize gamete: \(n = \frac{20}{2} = 10\).
Apple gamete: \(n = \frac{34}{2} = 17\).

Step 3: Final Answer
The missing values in order are 24, 16, 10, and 17.

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q27 - Gamete transfer and excess male gametes in simple plants

questiontext.text: In several simple plants such as algae, bryophytes, and pteridophytes, why is the number of male gametes produced several thousand times greater than the number of female gametes?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In algae, bryophytes, and pteridophytes, water serves as the medium through which male gametes move to reach the stationary female gametes.

Step 2: Evaluation
During transport through water, a large number of male gametes fail to reach the female gametes. To compensate for this loss of male gametes during transport, the number of male gametes produced is several thousand times the number of female gametes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Excess male gametes are produced to compensate for the heavy loss of male gametes during transport through water.

answer.text: Multiple male gametes must fuse with a single egg to form a diploid zygote
Female gametes are motile and actively escape from male gametes
To compensate for the loss of a large number of male gametes that fail to reach the female gametes during transport through water
Because male gametes are formed by mitosis while female gametes are formed by meiosis

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q28 - Gamete motility exceptions and pollen tubes in seed plants

questiontext.text: In a majority of organisms, the male gamete is motile and the female gamete is stationary. Which statement correctly identifies the exceptions to this pattern?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Gamete motility varies across different groups of organisms depending on their mechanism of gamete transfer.

Step 2: Evaluation
In a few fungi and algae, both types of gametes are motile. On the other hand, in seed plants (gymnosperms and angiosperms), the male gametes are non-motile and are carried to the female gamete (egg) inside the ovule by pollen tubes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Both gametes are motile in a few fungi and algae, whereas in seed plants non-motile male gametes are carried to the female gamete by pollen tubes.

answer.text: In all bryophytes, both male and female gametes are motile, whereas in algae only female gametes are motile
In seed plants, motile male gametes swim through water to reach the ovule
In reptiles and birds, both sperm and ovum are motile inside the female body
In a few fungi and algae both types of gametes are motile, whereas in seed plants non-motile male gametes are carried by pollen tubes

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q29 - Pollination in self-fertilising versus cross-pollinating plants

questiontext.text: Why is the transfer of pollen grains to the stigma relatively easy in bisexual, self-fertilising plants such as peas?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In seed plants, pollen grains produced in anthers are the carriers of male gametes and must be transferred to the stigma before fertilisation can occur.

Step 2: Evaluation
In bisexual, self-fertilising plants like peas, the anthers and stigma are located close to each other. Consequently, pollen grains soon after they are shed come in contact with the stigma, unlike in cross-pollinating and dioecious plants that rely on pollination across separate flowers or individuals.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Pollen transfer is relatively easy in peas because the anthers and stigma are located close to each other.

answer.text: Anthers and stigma are located close to each other
The plants are dioecious and release pollen into water
Pollen grains are motile and swim to the stigma
Fertilisation occurs without pollen tube germination

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q30 - Parthenogenesis in animals

questiontext.text: In organisms such as rotifers, honeybees, some lizards, and turkey, the female gamete develops into a new organism without fertilisation. This phenomenon is known as:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
While syngamy (fusion of male and female gametes) is the most vital event of sexual reproduction, certain animals exhibit an alternative pathway.

Step 2: Evaluation
When the female gamete undergoes development to form a new organism without fertilisation, the phenomenon is called parthenogenesis. It is observed in rotifers, honeybees, and even some lizards and birds (turkey).

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Development of a female gamete into a new organism without fertilisation is called parthenogenesis.

answer.text: Syngamy
Parthenogenesis
Embryogenesis
Sporulation

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q31 - External fertilisation characteristics and disadvantage

questiontext.text: Which of the following is a major disadvantage of external fertilisation as observed in bony fishes and frogs?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In external fertilisation (seen in most algae, bony fishes, and amphibians), syngamy occurs in the external medium (water) outside the body of the organism.

Step 2: Evaluation
Organisms exhibiting external fertilisation show great synchrony between the sexes and release a large number of gametes into water to enhance the chances of syngamy, producing a large number of offspring. However, a major disadvantage is that the offspring are extremely vulnerable to predators, threatening their survival up to adulthood.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The major disadvantage of external fertilisation is that the offspring are extremely vulnerable to predators.

answer.text: There is a lack of synchrony between the sexes during gamete release
Very few offspring are produced due to low gamete numbers
The offspring are extremely vulnerable to predators, threatening their survival up to adulthood
Zygotes formed in water are haploid and cannot undergo mitosis

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q32 - Internal fertilisation and gamete numbers

questiontext.text: Which statement accurately characterises organisms exhibiting internal fertilisation?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In many terrestrial organisms (fungi, reptiles, birds, mammals) and a majority of plants (bryophytes, pteridophytes, gymnosperms, angiosperms), syngamy occurs inside the body of the organism (internal fertilisation).

Step 2: Evaluation
In internal fertilisation, the egg is formed inside the female body where it fuses with the male gamete. Although the number of sperms produced is very large, there is a significant reduction in the number of eggs produced. In seed plants, non-motile male gametes are delivered by pollen tubes.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
In organisms with internal fertilisation, the egg is formed inside the female body, sperm production remains very large, and there is a significant reduction in the number of eggs produced.

answer.text: It occurs exclusively in mammals and angiosperms
Both the number of sperms and the number of eggs produced are significantly increased compared to external fertilisation
The egg is released into the external medium while sperms remain inside the male body
The egg is formed inside the female body, and while sperm numbers are very large, there is a significant reduction in the number of eggs produced

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q33 - Fate of zygote in fungi, algae, and haplontic life cycle

questiontext.text: In organisms belonging to fungi and algae, what happens to the diploid zygote before germination, and how does it divide in organisms with a haplontic life cycle?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Formation of the diploid zygote is universal in all sexually reproducing organisms, but its further development depends on the organism's life cycle and environment.

Step 2: Evaluation
In fungi and algae, the zygote develops a thick wall that is resistant to desiccation and damage, and it undergoes a period of rest before germination. In organisms with a haplontic life cycle, the diploid zygote divides by meiosis to form haploid spores that grow into haploid individuals.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
The zygote develops a thick resistant wall, rests before germination, and in haplontic life cycles divides by meiosis to form haploid spores.

answer.text: It develops a thick wall resistant to desiccation and damage, undergoes a period of rest, and in haplontic life cycles divides by meiosis to form haploid spores
It immediately divides by mitosis to form a diploid embryo without any resting period
It secretes a calcareous shell and undergoes incubation outside the water
It remains haploid and divides by mitosis to form gametes

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q34 - Processes occurring during embryogenesis

questiontext.text: During embryogenesis, which two key cellular processes transform the single-celled zygote into an embryo with specialised tissues and organs?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Embryogenesis refers to the process of development of an embryo from the zygote, which is the vital link ensuring continuity of species across generations.

Step 2: Evaluation
During embryogenesis, the zygote undergoes cell division (mitosis) to increase the number of cells in the developing embryo, and cell differentiation, which helps groups of cells undergo modifications to form specialised tissues and organs.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Embryogenesis involves mitotic cell division and cell differentiation.

answer.text: Meiosis and syngamy
Mitotic cell division and cell differentiation
Encystation and sporulation
Gametogenesis and pollination

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q35 - Oviparous versus viviparous animals and survival of young ones

questiontext.text: Why are the chances of survival of young ones greater in viviparous organisms (such as most mammals) than in oviparous organisms (such as reptiles and birds)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
Animals are categorised into oviparous and viviparous based on whether the development of the zygote takes place outside or inside the body of the female parent.

Step 2: Evaluation
In oviparous animals like reptiles and birds, fertilised eggs covered by a hard calcareous shell are laid in a safe place in the environment and hatch after incubation, leaving them exposed to environmental hazards and predators. In viviparous animals, the zygote develops into a young one inside the body of the female organism and is delivered after attaining a certain stage of growth, providing proper embryonic care and protection.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
Survival chances are greater in viviparous organisms because the embryo develops inside the female body with proper embryonic care and protection.

answer.text: Viviparous animals lay fertilised eggs covered by a hard calcareous shell
Viviparous animals produce a much larger number of offspring per reproductive cycle
The zygote develops inside the female body, ensuring proper embryonic care and protection
Viviparous animals exhibit external fertilisation in protected aquatic habitats

name.text: NEETUG_BIOLOGY_REPRODUCTIONINORGANISMS_STANDARDMCQ_Q36 - Post-fertilisation changes in a flower

questiontext.text: Which of the following accurately describes the post-fertilisation fate of floral parts in angiosperms?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Conceptual Principle
In flowering plants, the zygote is formed inside the ovule, and fertilisation triggers coordinated changes in the floral structures.

Step 2: Evaluation
After fertilisation, the sepals, petals, and stamens of the flower generally wither and fall off, while the pistil remains attached to the plant. The zygote develops into the embryo, the ovules develop into the seeds, and the ovary develops into the fruit, which forms a thick protective wall called the pericarp.

Step 3: Final Conclusion
After fertilisation, sepals, petals, and stamens wither and fall off, the pistil remains attached, the zygote forms the embryo, ovules form seeds, and the ovary forms the fruit with its protective pericarp.

answer.text: Sepals, petals, and pistil fall off, while stamens remain attached to form the pericarp
The ovule develops into the fruit, and the ovary matures into the seed
The zygote develops into the pericarp, and the pistil withers away
Sepals, petals, and stamens wither and fall off; the pistil remains attached; the zygote becomes the embryo, ovules become seeds, and the ovary becomes the fruit with a protective pericarp
